results.title: Fairness Metrics
results.content: AI fairness evaluation involves using a set of mathematical tools to measure and address bias in AI models. These tools assess how fairly AI systems treat different demographic groups, focusing on concepts like equal opportunity, demographic parity, and group fairness. Think of fairness metrics as a set of ethical guidelines for AI, similar to how building codes ensure equal access for everyone. Each metric highlights a different aspect of fairness, reflecting the reality that fairness in AI isn't one-size-fits-all — it requires multiple perspectives to ensure equity across groups. By using these tools, companies can comply with regulations, build trust with diverse customers, and protect their brand reputation. Organizations employ fairness metrics to build more equitable AI systems. These early efforts focused on demographic parity and equal opportunity, establishing foundations for ethical AI evaluation.Recent developments have expanded fairness metrics to address intersectional bias and context-specific equity concerns. Fairness Metrics quantify bias and discrimination in AI systems.

results.title: Top 7 Fairness Metrics in Machine Learning
results.content: Top 7 Fairness Metrics in Machine Learning Explore essential fairness metrics in machine learning that help ensure equitable AI systems and mitigate bias across diverse groups. **Machine learning models impact critical decisions, so ensuring they treat everyone fairly is essential.** Fairness metrics help identify and reduce bias, making AI systems more equitable. Here's a summary of seven key fairness metrics: * **Statistical Parity Difference (SPD):** Measures the difference in positive outcomes across groups. ### Definition and Formula The **Impact Ratio** is a metric used to assess fairness by comparing how different demographic groups experience positive outcomes. This metric helps ensure that the model performs consistently across different groups. ### Definition Group-Based Parity is a fairness metric in machine learning that evaluates whether different protected groups - such as those defined by gender, race, or age - receive similar outcomes from a model. ### Use Cases This metric is particularly relevant in areas like hiring, lending, and healthcare, where fair treatment across groups is essential: * **Hiring Systems**: Ensuring that algorithms evaluate candidates equitably, regardless of their demographic background. ### Real-World Implementation To address these limitations, implementing Group-Based Parity involves a few key steps: * **Balanced Training Data**: Ensuring the dataset represents all demographic groups fairly. Fairness metrics play a crucial role in ensuring AI models produce fair outcomes. When applying these metrics, focus on: * Testing thoroughly across diverse demographic groups * Updating models based on fairness evaluations * Keeping detailed records of bias mitigation efforts These steps help establish a solid foundation for creating fair AI systems. To stay ahead, organizations should: * Train models using balanced and representative data * Adjust models based on fairness metric results By embedding these practices into your development process, you can design AI systems that work fairly and effectively for all users. Ensuring fairness and minimizing bias in machine learning models is an ongoing process that requires regular monitoring and updates. Here are some key steps you can take: * **Evaluate fairness metrics regularly**: Use established fairness metrics, such as demographic parity or equalized odds, to measure and track potential biases in your model's predictions.

As we have seen before, the hiring model does not satisfy equal opportunity, as the false negative rates differ between sensitive groups. The equal calibration fairness metric requires that the model is equally calibrated for each sensitive group. Second, in cases where fairness is relevant, it is not uncommon that base rates \(p\_a = P(Y=1 \mid A=a)\) (i.e., the proportion of positives) are different across groups, meaning that \(A\) and \(Y\) are not independent. If base rates differ across groups (i.e., \(p\_a \neq p\_b\)), it is impossible for demographic parity and equal calibration to hold at the same time. A probabilistic interpretation of demographic parity requires that the model’s predictions are independent of sensitive group membership, i.e., \(A \perp\!\!\!\perp \hat{Y}\). Equal calibration, on the other hand, requires that, conditional on the model’s predictions, the ground truth labels are independent of sensitive group membership, i.e., \(A \perp\!\!\!\perp Y \mid \hat{Y}\). As such, demographic parity and equal calibration *cannot* hold when base rates are unequal across groups. If base rates differ across groups (i.e., \(p\_a \neq p\_b\)) and risk scores \(R\) are not independent of target variable \(Y\), it is impossible for demographic parity and equalized odds to hold at the same time. Equalized odds requires that, conditional on the ground truth labels, the model’s predictions are independent of sensitive group membership, i.e., \(\hat{Y} \perp\!\!\!\perp A \mid Y \). Provided that the (non-thresholded) risk scores \(R\) are not independent of the ground truth labels \(Y\) (i.e., the model’s predicted scores are somewhat sensible), increasing the decision threshold for group \(a\) inevitably increases the number of false positives in group \(a\) and hence the false positive rate. When a classifier does not have perfect accuracy and base rates differ across sensitive groups, it is impossible to satisfy equal calibration and equalized odds simultaneously.

results.title: AI fairness metrics | AI Governance Lexicon | VerifyWise
results.content: # AI fairness metrics. AI fairness metrics are quantitative measures used to evaluate whether an artificial intelligence system produces biased outcomes across different groups. These metrics assess how a model treats individuals based on sensitive attributes like race, gender, age or disability. Governance teams, regulators and auditors rely on fairness metrics to verify compliance with rules like the EU AI Act, NYC Local Law 144 and civil rights laws like ECOA. According to the World Economic Forum's 2023 Global AI Governance Survey, only 39% of AI systems in production are regularly tested for fairness across demographic groups. ### Types of AI fairness. Fairness in AI has multiple definitions because different contexts call for different ethical goals. Group fairness makes sure that different demographic groups receive similar treatment or outcomes. Individual fairness makes sure that similar individuals are treated similarly by the AI model. Each metric captures a different aspect of model behavior, which is why teams typically apply several in parallel.
